lesson.title: Why Nothing Stands Alone: The Principle of Comparison
lesson.summary: Comparison is the foundational principle that every well-designed experiment needs at least two groups so a treatment's effect can be measured against a baseline, since a single group's result cannot be interpreted on its own.
lesson.body:
Comparison is the foundational principle that every well-designed experiment must include at least two groups, typically a treatment group and a control group, so that the effect of a treatment can be measured relative to a baseline rather than judged in isolation. It is not simply good practice, it is a logical necessity: a single number describing what happened to one group, on its own, cannot tell you what would have happened without the treatment, so it cannot tell you what the treatment actually did.

The headache drug example from the previous section makes the necessity of comparison concrete. Observing that 71% of drug takers improved sounds impressive until you learn that 44% of subjects taking an inactive placebo improved too, revealing that a large share of that apparent success would have happened anyway. Without the comparison group, researchers would have had no way to separate the drug's genuine 27 percentage point contribution from the placebo effect and from headaches simply resolving on their own. This is the same logical gap that plagues observational studies without a comparison built in: a number by itself, no matter how large, is not evidence of an effect until it is compared against a baseline.

Comparison scales naturally to experiments with multiple factors and levels. In the earlier fertilizer and watering experiment with 4 treatment combinations, no single treatment's yield was interpretable alone, what mattered was comparing all 4 groups' average yields, 140, 148, 155, and 171 bushels per acre for low fertilizer with daily watering, low fertilizer with every-other-day watering, high fertilizer with daily watering, and high fertilizer with every-other-day watering respectively, against one another to see which combination produced the best results and whether the two factors interacted. The comparison across every treatment combination, not any single group's result, is what actually answers the experiment's question.

For a comparison to be meaningful, the groups being compared must be alike in every way except the treatment itself, which is why comparison in experiments is almost always paired with random assignment of units to treatment and control groups. If healthier subjects had been allowed to choose the real drug while sicker subjects were left in the placebo group, the resulting 27 percentage point gap would reflect pre-existing health differences as much as the drug, echoing the same lurking variable danger that produces Simpson's paradox when subgroups are not comparable to begin with.

Comparison is the thread running through everything in this unit: experiments exist because comparing manipulated groups can support causal claims that observational comparisons cannot, experimental units and subjects are what get divided into comparable groups, treatments defined by factors and levels are what differs between those groups, and control groups and placebos exist specifically to give the treatment group a fair, uncontaminated baseline to be compared against. Take away the principle of comparison, and every other piece of experimental design vocabulary loses its purpose.
